=== product-design/what-gets-read-aloud.md 1 A listener never hears a navigation label, and a paragraph with no real words, such as a section-break ornament, is silently dropped before synthesis. The audio opens with the article's title. The recipe leaves out a heading inside the body that only repeats the title, so a listener hears the title once. Some boilerplate still gets through: a footer donation ask or a sponsor mention arrives as ordinary prose sentences and nothing yet tells it apart from real content. 2 - **A comparison operator** reads as the word it stands for: `3 < 4` is heard as "three less than four," and a combined form like `<=` as "less than or equal to." === technical-design/article-extraction.md 1 The spoken form is derived from the unit's display markdown by walking its CommonMark token tree, so the display and spoken forms come from one extraction (invariant 1). A fenced code block becomes the fixed placeholder `"Code sample."`. A table's header row is spoken on its own line, then each body row as its own line of header-aware prose (`"Feature: Extraction, Status: done."`) rather than speaking pipe characters. A heading, a quote and the title unit are read as their words, without their markers. Every block inside a unit becomes its own line, so a unit carrying several paragraphs or list items never runs the last word of one into the first word of the next. A list item gets no full stop. An ordered item keeps its `1.` at the start of its line, and the spoken form does not announce nesting depth. A split list's resumed empty item (see [markdown-units](markdown-units.md)) has no spoken line at all. The derivation strips a task-list checkbox and reads struck-through text as its words, with no sign of the strike. Emphasis markers and link destinations are dropped throughout. 2 3 A shared tail, `sanitize_spoken`, then turns any leftover emphasis or code marker that touches text into a space, so the newlines between a unit's lines survive the pass. It drops the space a marker left before punctuation and collapses whitespace. It reduces an opening or closing tag around a word to the word inside (`` to "software", `` to "div"). A lone `<` or `>` is not a tag, so this step leaves it for the operator rule that follows. It accepts the escaped form of a tag as well, because the table linearizer reads a cell off the raw inline source, where the backslash still sits in front of the tag. A last pass turns a comparison-operator sequence into the word it stands for, longest match first: `<=` "less than or equal to", `>=` "greater than or equal to", `->` "to", `=>` "to", `<-` "from", `<<` "much less than", `>>` "much greater than", `<3` "heart", then the bare `<` "less than" and `>` "greater than". The describer's model output runs through the same tail (see [the-describer](the-describer.md)), since a JSON schema cannot forbid a marker inside its string value. 4 - **Quote voice switching.** A listener hears a quote in the one narrator voice, and nobody has yet validated the blockquote audio round-trip end to end. === technical-design/extraction-service.md 1 `run` executes the script inside a Dynamic Worker: the injection bundle carries cheerio, domino, turndown and its GFM plugin (`@truto/turndown-plugin-gfm`) with it, the article parses inside because the recipe's `$` must exist there, and what returns is JSON. The script's `toMarkdown` calls serialize each selected element with its own tag, so Turndown sees the tag that selects its markdown rule. `toMarkdown` also wraps a `
` with no `` child in `` before conversion. The validator is not part of the bundle; the mechanical checks run in the main Worker, so one implementation serves the workflow path and the agent tool path. Inside the same Dynamic Worker call, after the script returns, the runtime splits a list unit around any nested code block or image and prepends the title unit, and it returns both the declared units and the flattened ones. The validator checks the declared units; when they pass, `run` returns the flattened units (see [markdown-units](markdown-units.md)). A recipe that does not parse, throws against changed markup, or hangs until the CPU cap kills it, is a validation failure: the revision path's trigger, with its crash report as the validator report. A module that does not parse never starts the Dynamic Worker, so it cannot report itself as data; the load failure is recognised from the platform's own error, which names `recipe.js` in some runtimes and raises a bare `SyntaxError` in others. Only platform failures outside the recipe are `error` terminals: a Dynamic Worker that is unreachable, a bundle that does not load.
=== technical-design/recipes.md
     1	A recipe is a script plus the declarations around it. The container selector names the element that contains the article, and everything outside the container is site chrome. The inventory names every element kind the domain's pages carry inside the container and the role each plays: a unit, inline content, a wrapper, or the title. The ignores are the selectors deliberately excluded, each with the judgement that justified it; typical ignores are ads, date stamps and share rows. Every recipe excludes footnote markers and footnote bodies, because the authoring prompts instruct it to. The author prompt and the revision prompt embed one shared contract of plain instructions. The prompts also require GFM markdown and a formula written as its alttext with no delimiter. The recipe passes the whole element to `toMarkdown`, never a piece of it, and declares a whole list as one unit even when the list holds a code block or an image. They exclude a blockquote's attribution, a `
`, a heading self-link and a heading that repeats the title, and they keep a task list's checkboxes. See [markdown-units](markdown-units.md) for what each of those becomes in a unit's display.
     2	Units come back in document order, one element per unit as the recipe declares them, never overlapping: once an element is a unit, everything inside it is that unit's content. The kinds are `paragraph`, `code` and `image`. A paragraph is any flow that renders as markdown: prose, headings, quotes, lists, tables; a list is a single declared unit, even one holding a code block or an image. The fixed conversion pass produces a paragraph or code unit's display markdown. Before the units reach the API or the authoring agent's extract tool, the runtime splits a list unit around any embedded code block or image (see [markdown-units](markdown-units.md)). An image unit carries `src` and `alt` exactly as the page presents them: the recipe never invents `alt`, and the src is how the recipe resolves the domain's lazy-load conventions. An image the article carries is always emitted, even when its src cannot be resolved. Acquiring, validating, describing or dropping images is downstream's business.
     3	The same validator runs at authoring, revision and extraction. It checks that every unit's element is inside the container, in document order, none nested inside another; that every element kind in the container is declared or reported as unexpected; that no readable text is left after the units and ignores are removed, with the leftover report naming the element kinds that carry it; and that no declared unit is an `
  • ` on its own. The report line for an orphaned `
  • ` names the unit, the list it belongs to and the rule that a recipe hands a list over whole. It also checks that every unit's markdown is valid: non-empty, no residual HTML outside code, balanced fences. Invalid markdown fails a recipe like any other problem.
=== technical-design/markdown-units.md
     1	A unit's `display` is markdown. Every recipe hands its selected elements to one shared converter rather than converting by hand ([recipes](recipes.md)), so the mapping from source to markdown is the same across every domain. Inside the sandbox, the runtime splits list units and prepends the title after the recipe returns; the host then validates the declared units and returns the flattened units only when validation is clean, before anything crosses to the API or appears in the authoring agent's extract tool.
     2	> The runtime builds the title unit from `extraction.title` once it has every recipe-declared unit; the recipe does not select it. Building it this way is deterministic from the title the recipe already extracted, so it needs no judgement from the agent. The authoring prompts tell the agent to leave out any heading that repeats the title, so a recipe yields one title unit and the listener hears the title once (see [recipes](recipes.md) and [what-gets-read-aloud](../product-design/what-gets-read-aloud.md)).
     3	    A["Sandbox: recipe runs,
    declared units with
    paths, display from
    toMarkdown"] --> S["1 Split each list
    holding a pre or image,
    convert the parts,
    prepend # title"]
     4	    S --> H["2 Both lists
    return to the host"]
     5	    H --> V{"3 Validator on the
    declared units:
    inventory, leftover,
    nesting, orphaned li"}
     6	    V -->|Problems| R(("Report to the
    agent: revise"))
     7	    V -->|Clean| O(("4 Flattened units,
    also what the
    agent sees"))
     8	```
     9	
    10	`toMarkdown` passes the element itself, its own tag included, to Turndown with the fixed configuration (ATX headings, fenced code, `-` bullets, `---` rules) and the GFM plugin. Each Turndown rule fires only when its tag is present, so the tag selects the markdown construct: `h2` for a heading, `blockquote` for a quote, `ol` or `ul` for a list. `toMarkdown` wraps the content of a `
    ` with no `` child in `` before conversion, so every `
    ` becomes a fenced block.
    11	
    12	Inside the same sandbox run, once the recipe has returned its declared units, the runtime splits every list unit that holds a code block or an image, at any nesting depth (1). The split yields a list part, then the code or image unit, then the rest of the list, in document order. `toMarkdown` converts each list part with its own list tag intact. The runtime then prepends the title unit, only when the extracted title is not empty. Both lists return to the host (2): the declared units, each tied to its real element path, and the flattened units. The same validator runs at authoring, revision and extraction against the declared units only ([recipes](recipes.md)) (3). When it is clean, the flattened units are what the workflow returns and what an authoring or revising agent's extract tool shows (4) ([extraction-service](extraction-service.md)); when it reports problems, the host discards the flattened units.
    13	
    14	> [!NOTE] Why the validator reads the declared units and not the split ones
    15	> The validator's nesting check flags any two units whose paths sit inside one another. A list-part clone from the split has no path, because the clone was never part of the parsed article tree. Validating the declared units, which are still elements at real positions, means every path the validator checks is real, and a split part never needs one. The split runs in the sandbox because the converter lives there, so it happens before validation.
    16	
    17	> [!WARNING] The validator does not check that a unit kept its markdown
    18	> Inventory and leftover-text checks confirm that every element in the container is accounted for and that no readable text was dropped. Neither confirms that a unit's markdown syntax, such as a heading's `#`, a quote's `>` or a list's numbering, survived the conversion. A recipe whose converter drops the element's own tag therefore still validates clean. In production, 53 headings reached the listener's page as plain paragraphs, 16 quotes lost their `>` and every ordered list came out with bullets, and every recipe behind them had validated. Nothing downstream catches it either; the reader sees undifferentiated paragraphs, the table of contents finds no heading, and the audio sounds right.
    19	
    20	> [!TIP] Rejected: splitting a list by handing each item to the converter on its own
    21	> Turndown's list rule reads the parent `
      ` or `
        ` to number or bullet an item, so an item converted alone comes out with no ordinal and no bullet. The runtime instead keeps every surviving list part inside a clone of the original list's own tag, so Turndown still numbers or bullets the items in each part.
    22	
    23	> [!TIP] Rejected: wrapping a formula's alttext in `$…$` or `$$…$$`
    24	> `sanitize_spoken` has a rule for each markdown marker Turndown can emit and no rule for a dollar sign, so a delimiter would reach the audio as a literal character. The alttext carries no delimiter at all instead, and reads as plain words in both the display and the spoken form.
    25	
    26	## ⏩ What is not built yet
    27	
    28	- **Telling code apart from a non-code `
        `.** `toMarkdown` treats every `
        ` as code and wraps it in `` before conversion; nothing distinguishes a `
        ` used for plain preformatted layout.
    29	- **An empty declared element.** The runtime has no special handling for a recipe-declared unit that converts to no markdown.
